brief.topic: When the Shortest Route Looks Curved

s01: Two places sit at the same northern latitude.
On this flat map, the direct route looks like a horizontal line.
Yet a route that bows toward the pole is shorter on a sphere.
The map has changed what distance looks like.
Let us keep the same two places and put them on a globe.
The horizontal map line follows a circle of latitude.
Away from the equator,
that circle does not pass through the center of the sphere.
Now take the plane through both places and the sphere's center.
Its intersection with the surface is a great circle.

The shorter arc
between our two places
is the shortest surface route.
Notice that it curves on the map

because the map stretches
the surface.
In our example,

both places are
thirty five degrees north
and their longitudes differ
by one hundred and thirty degrees.
On a sphere of radius one,
following the latitude takes about one point eight six units.
The great circle takes about one point six seven.
That difference comes from the geometry, not a faster traveler.
A useful way to picture the theorem
is to rotate the globe

until the starting place
becomes the north pole.
A meridian reaches the destination without sideways wandering.
Any sideways motion adds length

without reducing the required
change in polar angle.
This explanation assumes a sphere

and a route constrained
to its surface.
Real flight planning also considers

winds, airspace,
and the Earth's shape.
A line that looks bent on a map

can be the simplest route
on the world.

scenes.narration: Two places sit at the same northern latitude. On this flat map, the direct route looks like a horizontal line. Yet a route that bows toward the pole is shorter on a sphere. The map has changed what distance looks like. Let us keep the same two places and put them on a globe. The horizontal map line follows a circle of latitude. Away from the equator, that circle does not pass through the center of the sphere. Now take the plane through both places and the sphere's center. Its intersection with the surface is a great circle. The shorter arc between our two places is the shortest surface route. Notice that it curves on the map because the map stretches the surface. In our example, both places are thirty five degrees north and their longitudes differ by one hundred and thirty degrees. On a sphere of radius one, following the latitude takes about one point eight six units. The great circle takes about one point six seven. That difference comes from the geometry, not a faster traveler. A useful way to picture the theorem is to rotate the globe until the starting place becomes the north pole. A meridian reaches the destination without sideways wandering. Any sideways motion adds length without reducing the required change in polar angle. This explanation assumes a sphere and a route constrained to its surface. Real flight planning also considers winds, airspace, and the Earth's shape. A line that looks bent on a map can be the simplest route on the world.
